item.title: Does AI actually save employees time? Data is contradictory
item.description:
It’s early days for AI-assisted work, and sentiments are mixed about its benefits: Does AI actually bring value and save employees time, or does it bog them down and add unnecessary activities?

Data from ActivTrak seems to vacillate between those two potential realities: The latest research from the productivity tracking software company says employees who use AI most heavily are working up to 90 minutes longer each day, yet its previous research, published earlier this year, found that they are actually working less.

The discrepancy may be due in part to the timespan and sample sizes of the data collection for the two reports, but it indicates that enterprises should still be wary of vendor claims about AI-related productivity gains. Measuring them remains incredibly difficult.

AI use compared

ActivTrak’s current findings are based on behavioral work data gathered from 9,140 knowledge workers across 467 enterprises over a five month period (April 1 to September 25, 2026). This sample is much smaller than that of its previous report based on 443 million hours of work performed by 163,638 employees across 1,111 organizations over a three year period (January 1, 2023 through December 31, 2025).

According to the latest findings, heavy AI users are working between 8.42 and 9.08 hours per day, compared to 7.58 hours for those not using AI. This contradicts ActivTrak’s previous finding that average workdays had decreased by roughly 9 minutes (a 2% decline) thanks to AI.

On the productivity front, heavy AI users have 22% shorter focus sessions than light users (37.8 minutes versus 48.2), suggesting their work is more fragmented due to AI use; further, they switch apps 15% more frequently.

“Over time, those interruptions add friction to high-value work that requires concentration, critical thinking, and sustained attention,” Sarah Altemus, manager of the ActivTrak Productivity Lab, said in a blog post describing the latest findings.

ActivTrak’s previous report had found that over the period of the earlier study, focus efficiency, the percentage of work time spent in focused, uninterrupted activity, fell to a three year low of 60% with AI use, and average focused session time in 2025 declined by 9% from 2023. However, that same report found that daily productive time increased by 19 minutes, or 5%, to 6 hours and 36 minutes, with AI in the workplace. Furthermore, productive sessions grew by 13%.

The company’s latest report also tracked the productivity differences between users of tools with embedded AI and users of web-based AI tools. Those using embedded AI switched apps 0.6 times an hour, while those using AI on the web switched between 1.7 and 4.2 times per hour. That’s up to 4x more switching than by employees who don’t make use of AI at all, which creates what ActivTrak describes as a “swivel-chair tax” — the additional effort spent by employees due to the movement between apps.

Similarly, in its previous report, ActivTrak had found that this multitasking rose 12%, or 10-plus minutes, with AI.

Interestingly, according to the latest research, light users spend more active work time in core job-specific apps (81.4% compared to 78%). “In other words, more frequent AI engagement doesn’t necessarily translate into more focused work,” Altemus pointed out.

The larger issue is the way organizations manage the additional capacity that AI may create, Altemus noted. “When employees complete tasks faster, managers may assume they have room for more responsibilities,” she said. Without clear workload boundaries, time savings may be redirected into additional work that can be taxing.

The numbers often don’t tell the full story

ActivTrak has a useful view of how work moves across applications, noted Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, but he also pointed out that it sells the capability that produces these measurements.

Recorded use depends on what the instrumentation can detect, he observed. For example, an employee can use AI at work and still appear in the non-user group, and work on an unmanaged personal device sits outside the measured estate. In addition, an API or a background agent can finish work without producing a desktop session, and passive screen time, an offline meeting captured through a calendar, and paid hours are also different measures. Furthermore, switching apps is easier to observe than switching attention within an application.

Ultimately, he noted, those judging the value of AI need to establish what happened after the first task became faster. “An improvement per paid hour can conceal effort left off the timesheet,” said Gogia. “The [enterprise] board should be able to say whose day improved and whose work made that improvement possible.”

item.title: Salesforce acquires Rune Technologies to add offline capabilities to Missionforce
item.description:
Salesforce is in the process of acquiring US-based defense-tech startup Rune Technologies to add offline capabilities to Missionforce, its Agentforce avatar for national security, defense, aerospace, and government agencies.

The startup’s TyrOS platform will be used to extend Missionforce into frontline military logistics, enabling deployed units to forecast supply requirements, optimize resource allocation, and make operational decisions even when network connectivity is unavailable, the CRM software provider said in a statement.

That is possible due to TyrOS’s offline-first architecture that caches last-known information about inventory, vehicles, and transportation routes using NFC-based hardware, allowing deployed units to access operational data without a continuous connection to centralized systems, according to the company’s website.

The platform can also exchange prioritized information between distributed nodes through a mesh network when connectivity becomes available, the website showed.

Currently, Missionforce acts as a system of record for personnel, equipment, and supplies across defense organizations, while providing tools for strategic planning.

For CIOs of defense organizations, the acquisition could mean improved operational continuity and better utilization of available resources, said Premal Shah, principal analyst at Avasant.

This would be helpful because frontline units could now continue to access critical logistics information and coordinate resource requirements during connectivity disruptions, rather than relying on manual records or waiting for centralized systems to become available, Shah added.

Once connectivity is restored, information can be synchronized across distributed nodes, helping headquarters regain visibility into frontline requirements and make more informed decisions about resource allocation and resupply, he further added.

However, implementing technologies such as TyrOS comes with its own set of risks, according to Pareekh Jain, principal analyst at Pareekh Consulting.

CIOs need to ensure that information updated by different military units while offline does not result in conflicting records when their systems reconnect, while also maintaining data security across distributed locations, Jain said.

TyrOS, though, is not an untested technology in military environments. Its platform is already deployed with the US Army and US Marine Corps, giving Rune an established presence in the defense sector, Salesforce said.

It plans to use the acquisition to build the foundation for a recent 10-year contract it won with the US Army, which has a $5.6 billion ceiling and focuses on modernizing military operations. The transaction is expected to close by April 2027.

item.title: 13 key questions shaping CIOs’ 2027 IT agendas
item.description:
With 2027 quickly looming, IT leaders should soon be finalizing their objectives for the new year, one certain to be rife with many unknowns if 2026 is any indication.

This year began with the call for a pivot from AI pilots to AI ROI, but questions around AI governance and accountability quickly took center stage as agentic AI made further inroads in the enterprise and high-profile incidents showed the risks of AI gone awry and the value of security-first approaches to AI agents.

Now, CIOs must anticipate how AI will evolve in 2027, how they’ll get their enterprises ready for all the risks and opportunities of that evolution, whether their teams will have the skills to seize on technology advances, and more.

To get a glimpse of how CIOs are approaching next year’s IT agenda, we asked IT leaders to share the key questions they are asking to shape their strategies for 2027. Here’s what they shared.

How do we ensure our AI investments provide tangible value as the cost calculus changes?

The big question as CIOs plot their IT agendas for 2027 still centers on providing verifiable business value, as 98% of CIOs report that board pressure to demonstrate measurable AI ROI has increased since 2024, according to a 2026 report based on a Dataiku/Harris Poll survey of 600 enterprise CIOs worldwide.

Doug Gilbert, CIO and chief digital officer at Sutherland, a digital transformation services company, is among those IT execs pondering this question as he executes his fiscal 2027 budget, which started in July.

“When I’m out speaking to people and they say, ‘It would be great if AI could do that,’ I say, ‘Yes, but would it provide value? Are we building value or are we just burning tokens?’” Gilbert says. He notes that he and his CIO peers are being increasingly judged on the outcomes they deliver for their organizations, meaning they have more incentive than ever to ensure the technology initiatives they undertake deliver ROI.

But the calculus on that is getting trickier than it was at the beginning of 2026 — in part because AI total cost of ownership (TCO) is challenging to calculate, but also because an AI pricing reset is on the horizon. So, to that end, CIOs such as Gilbert are now thinking about what level of ROI is high enough to justify the investment.

That’s a key question to ask now and into 2027, Gilbert says, particularly as the cost of tokens continues to rise. An AI use case that provides marginal ROI could stop producing any value in the near future if tokens increase even slightly, he notes.

As a result, Gilbert is working to factor in those dynamics when he and his team work with the business to identify which AI use cases to pursue — and he expects to do so even more moving forward. “I plan to pay a tremendous amount of time thinking about whether [a proposed project] is the right one to pursue,” he says, to ensure “when you put math on paper there is value with the project.”

How do we ensure observability and auditability of our AI systems?

According to a 2026 survey from OneStream, 47% of senior finance and IT executives say they have made a material business decision based on inaccurate, incomplete, or outdated financial data in the past 12 months.

Citing that statistic, Gilbert says he’s also asking critical questions about the observability and auditability of all of Sutherland’s AI uses cases. He wants to be sure he, other executives, and users are confident the company’s AI systems always have high-quality data — and thus accurate outputs. And he wants IT to achieve that observability and auditability so that the company can accurately track, measure, and improve its AI deployments over time.

“We will not deploy any AI that we can’t observe,” he says, a policy that he put in place about a year ago and will continue in 2027.

A wide range of tools under the moniker “AgentOps” are emerging to help IT leaders monitor AI activity, tools, and costs, starting with observability.

How do we move to more autonomous agentic processes?

“The challenge most technology executives are grappling with at the moment is how you move AI from human-assisted agentic to much more autonomous agentic processes with minimal human intervention or supervision,” says Jody Fullman, CIO of Reconomy and recently recognized as one of the UK’s top 100 CIOs in the CIO 100 UK Awards 2026.

Moreover, how do you achieve that securely and in a way that’s economically viable? he asks.

Fullman is implementing strategies to address this challenge. He is strengthening IT’s agentic controls by aligning Reconomy’s governance program to an industry-recognized framework. He is also implementing tools to monitor and manage tokens. And he’s moving some AI workloads to lower-costs models.

All that, he says, will set up the organization to develop and deliver more autonomous agentic capabilities ahead, noting that he and his team have been transitioning successful proof-of-concept agentic initiatives into MVPs to put the company on the path to more autonomous agentic processes.

How should OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident shape my security strategy?

Security has been a central factor in IT agendas for years. But Jeff Stovall, CIO for Dallas, Texas, says the 2026 Hugging Face incident, in which autonomous AI agents built by OpenAI escaped their sandbox testing environment and hacked into the infrastructure of AI open platform company Hugging Face, has him adjusting his plans for 2027.

“Hugging Face demonstrated that there was a lot more peril in the world of AI as it relates to cybersecurity than what we were ramping up for,” he says. “There’s now this notion that AI may have more downside for us than upside for us in the near future,” he adds, explaining that AI-fueled threats to the organization are more significant than the positives its use brings.

“In the upcoming six months to a year, what I see is that we have to take a hard turn in thinking about how AI poses a significant malevolent threat to our organization when wielded by actors seeking to do harm,” Stovall says. He points specifically to hackers’ ability to use AI to create swarms of bots that can autonomously collaborate and exploit all vulnerabilities nearly instantaneously and all at once. “That’s a dramatic acceleration and amplification to the threats we face.”

In response, Stovall says he’s shifting more resources to maturing his security program in 2027 than he initially budgeted — drawing funds away from internal AI deployments to “shore up the walls even further” by adding more AI automation and agents to have “much more machine speed in security response.”

How do we use AI to transform?

Marco Bill, SVP and CIO at Red Hat, believes using AI for productivity gains is now table stakes. So as he develops his plans for IT for 2027, he’s looking to push that notion even further, asking how the company can use AI to transform processes as a whole.

“This question helps me to keep reminding ourselves that we’re not just here to do IT. It’s more of a guiding principle,” he says.

And that in turn is underscoring the importance of transforming the IT organization into a more collaborative and business-centric one.

As an example of what’s brewing at Red Hat, Bill points to the work his IT team is doing with the company’s sales team to devise ways to use AI to enable account managers to have better conversations with customers to close deals faster. IT is also working with the marketing department to make go-to-market process more powerful, and his teams are adding agentic AI to their own IT operations to create fully autonomous workflows that cost less to run and manage.

All told, Bill and the IT team at Red Hat are building further on the work many CIOs began in 2026 by helping to reimagine business processes to reap AI benefits and bringing AI transformation home to IT workflows.

How do we empower users to transform their work with AI?

“Citizen AI” is a rising trend in the enterprise, and this is something Reconomy’s Fullman will continue to address in 2027, explaining that his company has found that much of its “success with AI was not by being a tech project but by empowering our users and business colleagues to transform their work and processes with AI.”

Fuller believes that his company will see more AI-enabled transformation, and see that transformation faster, by continuing to put more AI in the hands of users throughout the organization instead of expecting IT workers to become experts in all the processes that could be transformed by AI.

As such, Fuller says the upcoming year’s IT plans will continue to put AI tools in the hands of the users, and do so with governance, security, and transparency in place. He’ll also leverage the skills of workers in process transformation roles, which were recently created and installed in Reconomy’s business units but still work closely with IT architecture and data teams.

“They’re plugged into tech and the business to make sure we’re prioritizing the right things and doing things the right way as we drive transformation,” he explains.

How do we prevent our AI governance council from becoming a bottleneck?

Company leaders at intelligent automation platform provider Celigo want every team to build with AI, something CIO Amy Farrow knows makes security and controls critical. But Farrow also wants to make sure she enables speed and doesn’t unnecessarily slow down innovation, noting that barriers could lead to shadow AI.

“If [teams] all have to wait too long, they’ll find a way around the process,” she says.

To ensure that governance isn’t a bottleneck, Farrow explains that her “governance council doesn’t approve projects. It sets the rules: risk tiers, design criteria, a checklist every agent has to pass.”

She adds: “The teams approve their own work against those rules, and we audit. My team owns the integrations, access controls, and observability. My job is making it faster to build the right way.”

What controls do we need to put in place for AI agents?

As AI agents increasingly enter enterprise workflows, IT leaders will need to the level of permissions agents should be granted relative to the people on whose behalf those agents will be operating.

Farrow, who previously served as global CIO at Infoblox and Lyft, believes agents should resolutely have fewer permissions than the people whose tasks they will be performing.

“Someone in finance can issue a credit or update our ERP because we trust their judgment. An agent doesn’t get that by default,” she explains. “We start every agent with the least autonomy required to achieve the outcome. It can interpret a request or recommend an action. Changes to records go through checks the model can’t override, and bigger changes need a person to sign off.”

This approach also has a fiscal benefit, she says, noting, “Less autonomy means fewer model calls, which keeps costs in check.”

As AI increasingly goes agentic, CIOs will increasingly need to plan for ways to address this issue in the year ahead.

What happens when vendor agents start acting inside our systems?

“Many of our SaaS vendors are shipping agents, and some can make changes to our data by default,” Farrow says of another key security- and governance-related question many CIOs are facing. “For 2027, I want vendor agents held to the same standard as any other integration.”

Farrow has other questions related to the rapid rise in vendor agents, asking, “What can they touch? Can we see what they did?”

IT leaders need to ensure they can answer those types of questions, noting that California’s and Colorado’s new rules on automated decisions start in January. She wants to be able to give strong answers to those questions, stressing that “‘the vendor’s agent did it’ is not a defensible answer.”

How do we meet immediate business needs while building a foundation for growth?

Mieko Shibata, CIO at R&T Deposit Solutions, sees this as “the overarching question” for him as CIO.

“That question guides our investment decisions and how we allocate our team’s time,” she explains. “Our strategic direction is consistent, but each year’s agenda must balance immediate business priorities with progress toward our longer-term technology foundation. We consider both the value each investment delivers and how it contributes to the environment we are building.”

Shibata is taking a multiprong approach in her response to that overarching question.

First, she’s ensuring technology modernization turns into measurable business value and that modernization initiatives are prioritized based on that value.

She is also considering how IT responds to growth opportunities while keeping its longer-term transformation on track. “Our response is to consider the immediate commercial value alongside the longer-term technology implications. Can we reuse the capability? Will it scale? What will it take to support? Does it help simplify our environment?” she says.

And she’s thinking about how the company prepares for AI’s evolution while maintaining clear accountability for its use. “For 2027, my focus is on building a repeatable approach to evaluating and adopting AI as it evolves, with clear business benefits, appropriate controls, and accountability for the results,” she says.

Is our AI vision ambitious enough?

For Lauren Wilkinson, CIO for financial advisor services at Vanguard, AI ambition is top of mind as she develops her IT strategy for 2027.

AI strategy should accelerate the business strategy and “push leaders to reconsider what outcomes with AI are possible, rather than simply finding ways to make today’s processes faster or more efficient,” she says.

“It helps to start with an aspirational business vision, including what a few big outcomes could look like. Then you can work backward to determine where AI and technology can fundamentally change what is possible,” she explains.

In her work with financial advisors, she’s found that they’re primarily using AI to support administrative tasks such as drafting emails, conducting research, and taking meeting notes. But she sees an opportunity to build on those use cases in the upcoming year to deliver on that objective for a more ambitious AI program.

Like many CIOs, Wilkinson wants to take AI to the next level at her organization and ensuring that ambition is high enough is paramount to achieving that goal.

Do we have the talent to win in an AI-native world?

Wilkinson believes how CIOs address the AI talent question will be critical for organizational success.

“As AI continues to evolve, the skills that differentiate great technologists will also evolve, placing an even greater premium on AI expertise and deep business acumen,” she says. “CIOs should be building teams that understand the business, can identify the highest-value problems, and know how to orchestrate AI-native workflows to solve them at dramatically greater speed. The differentiator won’t simply be who has access to the best AI, but who has the people who know where and how to apply it.”

Most CIOs know this, so it is not surprising that this year’s State of the CIO survey found that AI tops the lists for both most sought-after skills and the hardest to find. As a result, CIOs will have to get creative to build up their teams’ AI know-how in the year ahead.

How should IT be reshaped to maximize value creation?

CIOs, including Shelia Anderson, EVP and chief information and digital officer at Unum Group, are also asking how they should shape IT as an organization to ensure they can deliver value to the business.

“That has been a big focus for us this year and will continue to move down that path in 2027,” she says.

The question has shaped Anderon’s work at Unum Group since she started in her role in May 2025. She has organized her IT department around end-to-end value streams and says that approach has helped her IT staff work more closely with the business and more readily identify where improvements can be made. She also has her IT organization working to better understand business processes, and has been working on building more capabilities to measure and manage AI costs as Unum seeks to transform using AI. And she’s looking at what investments and improvements are needed in IT’s foundation.

All these moves will enable the IT department to get better at value creation, Anderson says.

She plans to augment this work in the coming year by providing AI training and education for IT workers and employees throughout the company “so they know how they can drive value and find opportunities in their everyday use of AI.”

Ensuring she has the right mix of talent — meaning she has the right skills in the right seats to deliver value — will also shape the actions she takes as CIO in 2027, Anderson says.

“In 2025 and 2026 there was a lot of testing and learning, but 2027 will be a year of maturing. You’ll see more formal processes and settling in around how you’re going to leverage the skills in your organization to drive value,” she adds.

item.title: Collaboration: every CIO’s most underrated competitive advantage
item.description:
In Foundry’s 2026 State of the CIO survey, 83% of CIOs say their role is becoming more of a hybrid to lead both business and tech initiatives, rather than simply manage IT. As the two become more inseparable, the CIOs who see collaboration as a competitive advantage are putting daylight between them and those who see it as a cursory soft skill. And C-suites are responding as they rely more on IT to drive growth and accelerate efficiencies. So the CIOs who deliver the most value will bring collaboration skills to drive change and technical expertise.

Silos between IT and the business are falling

As the World Economic Forum notes, not every tech initiative requires deep collaboration. But as businesses move beyond routine IT investments into cross-functional, innovation-focused transformations, collaboration becomes essential.

For example, how can IT decisions help an organization open new markets faster, or emerging technologies reduce risk in areas like data privacy. It’s no surprise, then, that Deloitte found that 65% of CIOs reported directly to CEOs in 2025, up from 41% in 2015.

Because tech is now part of almost every business decision, it takes everyone’s expertise and insights — from the CIO to the CFO — to see the full picture of how an initiative will affect the company. Shared knowledge leads to better-informed decisions that give tech its biggest impact.

When silos persist, CIOs struggle to get buy-in for their initiatives. Protiviti’s Global Transformation survey found that while 61% of CIOs report being confident in their tech transformation outcomes, only 34% of CEOs and boards feel the same — and the gap is even wider for AI implementations.

That gap is, at its core, a collaboration problem. Without effective collaboration and communication, others can’t see the value of transformation efforts. CIOs who excel in these areas can more easily demonstrate value, win buy-in and keep their organizations at the forefront of technology.

Delivering speed and innovation

Collaboration goes well beyond getting buy-in. While it may be thought to slow IT down, it actually brings in the insights that make change more effective and faster.

As I’ve highlighted in the past, when organizations move away from rigid data ownership, cross-functional teams can share what drives further innovation.

The same holds across the C-suite. Perspectives from outside IT show CIOs how a tech implementation works for the company as a whole, and where new opportunities lie. That lets CIOs test, refine, and reshape solutions faster.

Most importantly, when teams share a common purpose and goals, everyone stays aligned on the best overall outcome for the business. Iteration happens much quicker because everyone is focused on the big picture rather than individual agendas. With increasingly rapid tech cycles, that speed is a competitive advantage in its own right.

Building your collaborative abilities

For CIOs used to the old way of doing things, shifting to a collaborative mindset can be a challenge. But like any capability, it can be developed and improved by applying some fundamental principles.

Earn trust through follow-through. Trust isn’t built at a kickoff meeting or with a mission statement. It’s built when people see you do what you said you would, again and again. For CIOs, that means delivering on commitments or flagging early when you can’t. Clear and consistent communication is one of the most reliable ways to build trust across an organization.

Make transparency the default, especially when news is bad. Transparency means more than status reports. It means being candid about costs, risks, trade-offs, and setbacks before they surprise anyone. When leaders sidestep difficult discussions, trust erodes and goals drift. And in technology programs, small unspoken issues have a way of becoming expensive ones.

Seek cultural fit in how you work, not who you are. Cultural fit isn’t about sameness or shared backgrounds. It’s about compatibility in management philosophy, values, decision-making, and communication. A CIO who values speed and experimentation, and a CFO who prioritizes predictability and control will clash unless both recognize the difference and agree on how to bridge it. The same is true when it comes to finding the best technology providers.

Focus on the what, not the how. Few things undermine collaboration faster than micromanagement. When leaders dictate how a colleague or partner should work, they signal distrust, stifle creativity and innovation, and tie up their own time policing activities instead of driving results. The better approach is to agree on clearly defined, measurable outcomes, and then step back. Letting go of the how isn’t giving up control but building enough trust that everyone gets there together.

This requires adjusting your workflows and skills, but the payoff is valuable insight from your collaborators and wins that lift the entire organization.

The new life of the CIO

The days when the CIO could simply be the tech expert behind the scenes are long gone. With AI and other technologies ingrained in every aspect of the business, the CIO must lead well beyond IT.

By making collaboration a priority, you can gain critical insights across teams to guide your tech strategy, and deliver the greatest value to your organization.

item.title: The middle layer will make or break enterprise AI agents
item.description:
The hype around AI agents and the models that power them is warranted. But while they can give organizations a real competitive advantage, in reality, how much value they deliver ultimately depends on something much less glamorous: the middleware and integrations that connect agents to systems across enterprise workflows.

Enterprises have used AI in various forms for decades, but agents represent a significant shift in how we put AI to work and what we ask it to do. The first phase of AI largely focused on generating, summarizing, analyzing and recommending information. Agents go a step further by executing actions and this is where the middle layer often gets overlooked.

Without the right APIs, MCPs, data streams, tools, deterministic logic, identity management and systems of record, agents and models essentially operate in a sandbox. As enterprises adopt agents into real-world workflows, the question CIOs need to ask isn’t simply, “Which AI agent should we deploy next?” It’s, “Can our enterprise faithfully support software action on our behalf?”

The model is becoming the commodity layer

After decades of leading a technology organization and countless implementations, I’ve seen firsthand how important it is to align technology with the business problems it is meant to solve. When it comes to AI agents, one of the biggest mistakes I see organizations make is setting unrealistic expectations for how a model will operate within their existing enterprise environment.

AI agents and models are often touted for what they can accomplish, which naturally focuses attention on their reasoning and execution capabilities. But we cannot simply layer them onto existing workflows and expect them to make decisions or take consistent, repeatable action reliably.

Financial services make for a great example of this. Think about an investing agent who evaluates companies using financial data. When they need it to calculate something precise, like a company’s cash burn ratio or runway, they don’t ask the LLM to do the math. Instead, they use a modern coding language such as python or node.js to perform deterministic analysis, then pass the results to the model to interpret their meaning in the broader context of the company.

As models continue to improve, the real differentiator isn’t the model itself, but what we engineer around them to turn their reasoning into trustworthy action.

The middle layer is where agents become enterprise software

For agents and models to deliver value outside a sandbox environment, they need connectivity to the enterprise systems supporting workflows. They also need to retrieve information from these systems, pass data between them and regularly execute actions within business-critical applications. 

Think of the middle layer as the connective tissue between reasoning and execution. The difference between an agent that can answer questions using information you’ve provided versus one that can retrieve a customer’s information, determine the appropriate next step and execute that action in a CRM or ERP system is fundamental. Building, managing and maintaining these connections across systems at scale requires a mature approach to integration.

Integration maturity varies across the enterprise landscape today. While some organizations have “point-to-point” technical debt, others have already developed mature AI integration infrastructure, investing in platforms such as Workato, MuleSoft or Apigee and building the engineering practices and dedicated teams needed to operate these connections. From what I’ve seen working with enterprise technology teams, it’s the latter that will find adding agents exponentially easier.

Another “gotcha” is how prominent MCP’s (Model Context Protocol) are becoming. MCP’s are quickly becoming the new standard for how Agents communicate with systems. There are hundreds already available within Enterprise AI tools such as Claude, Gemini or ChatGPT, but that still does not replace the need for an API/MCP management tool. B2B transactions will soon be performed via MCP or custom vibe-coded apps will need their own MCP to expose capabilities. Regardless, the technical requirement stays the same.

For organizations without a purpose-built foundation for connecting Agents with core systems, what starts as an AI initiative can actually turn into an integration modernization initiative. Before agents can reliably interact with systems, organizations need to connect them.

Agents will expose the technical debt we’ve learned to work around

Modernizing the connections between enterprise systems to prepare for agent integration can help us uncover critical gaps in our existing environments. We see where humans commonly pick up the slack between disconnected systems through manual processes like data unification or handoffs. Agents, however, cannot compensate for these inconsistencies in the same way.

Regardless of the type of AI model, if data is inaccessible, APIs are unreliable, business logic is undocumented or systems can’t communicate with each other, an agent’s capabilities are hindered. This doesn’t mean agents create new architectural problems; instead, they help us expose technical debt we’ve grown accustomed to. The danger is trying to recreate those human workarounds for individual agents rather than fixing the underlying problem.

As organizations deploy more agents, one-off fixes can snowball into novel integrations, data access patterns and workflows that IT teams have to maintain. Instead of reducing complexity, we risk adding another fragmented layer to the enterprise architecture.

Enterprise-grade agents require a different engineering discipline

Beyond these architectural challenges, Agentic AI integrations also inform software engineering. Unlike enterprise software, which is built around predictable inputs, deterministic logic and defined failure status, agents introduce probabilistic behavior into enterprise environments. This means that the same request can produce different outputs or actions depending on the context and information available to the model.

I’ve seen this play out in the enterprise environments we work with. Even relatively simple agentic workflows can become unreliable when connections are faulty, schedules are inconsistent or prompts drift over time. What looks straightforward from the outside can require significant engineering and oversight to operate reliably.

If a relatively simple, low-stakes workflow like this example is easily derailed, consider the engineering required when an agent is expected to take consequential action across ERP, CRM or financial systems. This is why real software engineering is necessary when integrating agents.

Enterprises can’t simply buy an agent and expect stable automation in the same way they might configure and deploy other platforms. Agents must operate as part of the whole system, often spanning multiple apps and requiring ongoing testing, monitoring and maintenance. This requires a team of dedicated engineers and developers to make agent behavior observable, recoverable and reliable enough for enterprise use.

CIOs need to build the organization around AI Agents

For CIOs, preparing your organization to scale agents requires looking beyond the technology itself. Mature integration practices and dedicated software engineering teams are important, but those capabilities need to be matched by strong technical leadership and a culture that understands software, data and calculated risk.

Strong technical leadership is especially important because, remember, not every workflow should be agentic. We need leaders to recognize where AI reasoning and adaptability create value and where conventional automation or deterministic software is the better choice. At the same time, teams need to be comfortable experimenting with probabilistic systems, learning from failures and pushing innovation without sacrificing the engineering discipline required for enterprise environments.

For CIOs, preparing your organization to scale agents requires four capabilities: mature integration practices, dedicated software engineering teams, strong technical leadership and a culture that understands software, data and calculated risk. These capabilities reinforce each other; having two or three isn’t enough. Organizations need all four to move beyond individual AI experiments and scale agents across the enterprise.

Enterprise connectivity has a new purpose

Enterprise connectivity used to enable information to move between systems. In the agentic era, it increasingly enables software to reason and act across them. Organizations can see improvement in operations and service delivery, but it depends on infrastructure that supports connectivity between systems.

With the right connections in place, agents can eliminate manual handoffs across complex workflows, accelerate decision-making and help organizations scale expertise and services without adding another layer to existing operations. That’s where I see the real competitive advantage emerging.

As agents and models become more capable and widely available, access to the technology itself will become less of a differentiator. What will separate organizations is their ability to build systems around Agentic AI, enabling it to work dependably across the systems that run their business.

The organizations that gain the greatest advantage from Agentic AI may not be those with the most agents deployed or even the best models, but those that have invested in the infrastructure, integration practices and engineering capabilities around them.
